standard.title: Equally and unequally likely outcomes
standard.description: List the possible outcomes of chance experiments involving equally likely outcomes and compare to those which are not equally likely
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can conduct repeated chance experiments and record results (AC9M4P02). They have not yet systematically listed all possible outcomes or compared equally and unequally likely situations.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students list the possible outcomes of chance experiments and compare equally likely with unequally likely outcomes.

nodes.label: Sample space
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can systematically list all possible outcomes of a chance experiment.
nodes.minimum_width: List all possible outcomes of a simple chance experiment (e.g. coin toss, single die roll); confirm the list is complete.
nodes.typical_width: List sample spaces for a variety of experiments including those with more outcomes (coloured spinners, card draws); use systematic listing strategies.
wider: List outcomes for two-stage experiments (coin + die)
Use a table or tree diagram to organise outcomes

response_modes.reason: Systematic listing requires a deliberate strategy (alphabetical, left-to-right, tree structure) to avoid omissions. Students who list unsystematically miss outcomes and subsequently misassign probabilities.

nodes.hinge_reason: Complete sample space enumeration is the prerequisite for Node 2 — students who miss outcomes assign probabilities that don't sum to 1 and cannot correctly identify equally likely conditions.
success_criteria: Student lists all outcomes of a given experiment without omissions
Student confirms the list is complete using a systematic approach

nodes.label: Equally likely outcomes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify when outcomes are equally likely and use this to describe the probability of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify that outcomes are equally likely for a fair experiment; describe the probability of each outcome as a fraction.
nodes.typical_width: Apply equally likely reasoning to fair coins, dice and spinners; express probabilities as fractions; explain why the fractions must sum to 1.
wider: Use equally likely outcomes to make predictions about repeated experiments
Investigate the Law of Large Numbers informally: why don't short runs match predictions?
success_criteria: Student correctly assigns equal probabilities to equally likely outcomes
Student expresses probability as a fraction and checks that all fractions sum to 1

nodes.label: Comparing equally and unequally likely outcomes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare experiments with equally likely outcomes to those with unequally likely outcomes and explain the difference.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify whether a given experiment has equally likely or unequally likely outcomes; explain the reason.
nodes.typical_width: Compare fair and biased spinners, weighted dice, and unequal colour bags; explain how unequal physical proportions produce unequal probabilities.
wider: Design an unequally likely spinner for a given purpose (e.g. a game that favours the player)
Investigate how First Nations probability games use unequal likelihood

response_modes.reason: Students tend to assume fairness by default. Varied physical contexts — spinners with unequal sectors, bags with unequal colour counts — challenge this assumption from multiple angles and build the discrimination.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Game design with unequal probabilities and cultural game contexts give advancing students rich, purposeful investigation material.
success_criteria: Student correctly classifies an experiment as equally or unequally likely
Student explains the physical source of the inequality in probabilities
